passage:
Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies in North America begin one of the most remarkable journeys in the insect world. Monarchs from the eastern United States and Canada fly as far as 4,800 kilometers south to a small area of mountain forests in central Mexico. There, they spend the winter crowded together on the branches of fir trees, sometimes so densely that the branches bend under their weight.

What makes this migration especially puzzling is that no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn belong to a special generation that can live for up to eight months. In contrast, monarchs born in early summer live for only a few weeks. In spring, the long-lived butterflies leave Mexico, fly north, lay eggs, and die. Their offspring continue the journey, and it takes three or four generations to return to Canada. As a result, the butterflies that arrive in Mexico each autumn have never been there before.

How do they find their way? Scientists have discovered that monarchs use the sun as a compass. Because the sun's position in the sky changes during the day, the butterflies must also keep track of time. Researchers found that a kind of internal clock in the monarchs' antennae allows them to adjust their direction as the hours pass. On cloudy days, monarchs may rely on Earth's magnetic field instead.

Unfortunately, the number of monarchs has declined sharply in recent decades. One major reason is the loss of milkweed, the only plant that monarch caterpillars can eat. Many students and families now help by planting milkweed in their gardens and schoolyards, giving the butterflies places to lay their eggs along their route.

passage:
Every autumn, millions of monarch butterflies in North America begin one of the most remarkable journeys in the insect world. Monarchs from the eastern United States and Canada fly as far as 4,800 kilometers south to a small area of mountain forests in central Mexico. There, they spend the winter crowded together on the branches of fir trees, sometimes so densely that the branches bend under their weight.

What makes this migration especially puzzling is that no single butterfly makes the whole round trip. The monarchs that fly south in autumn belong to a special generation that can live for up to eight months. In contrast, monarchs born in early summer live for only a few weeks. In spring, the long-lived butterflies leave Mexico, fly north, lay eggs, and die. Their offspring continue the journey, and it takes three or four generations to return to Canada. As a result, the butterflies that arrive in Mexico each autumn have never been there before.

How do they find their way? Scientists have discovered that monarchs use the sun as a compass. Because the sun's position in the sky changes during the day, the butterflies must also keep track of time. Researchers found that a kind of internal clock in the monarchs' antennae allows them to adjust their direction as the hours pass. On cloudy days, monarchs may rely on Earth's magnetic field instead.

Unfortunately, the number of monarchs has declined sharply in recent decades. One major reason is the loss of milkweed, the only plant that monarch caterpillars can eat. Many students and families now help by planting milkweed in their gardens and schoolyards, giving the butterflies places to lay their eggs along their route.

passage:
The Westbrook Weekly: Student News
Cafeteria Compost Project Cuts Trash in Half
by Daniel Ortiz, Grade 8 Reporter

Last September, the members of Westbrook Middle School's Green Team noticed a problem. After every lunch period, the cafeteria trash cans were overflowing with banana peels, apple cores, and uneaten bread. "We were throwing away food scraps that could have been useful," explained Green Team president Aisha Morgan. The team decided to start a composting program.

Composting is a natural process in which tiny living things, such as bacteria and worms, break down food scraps and turn them into rich soil. To get started, the Green Team placed three colored bins at the end of each lunch table: green for food scraps, blue for recycling, and gray for everything else. During the first few weeks, team members stood beside the bins to show students where each item belonged.

The beginning was not easy. Many students were in a hurry and threw everything into the gray bins. Some even complained that sorting took too much time. However, the Green Team did not give up. Members made posters, gave short talks in homeroom classes, and held a contest to see which grade could sort its trash most accurately. The seventh graders won a pizza party.

The results have been impressive. According to the school custodian, Mr. Hill, the cafeteria now fills only about half as many trash bags each day as it did last year. Meanwhile, the finished compost is being used in the school garden, where students grow lettuce, tomatoes, and herbs.

Next year, the Green Team hopes to share its program with two nearby elementary schools. "If we can do it here," Aisha said, "any school can."
stem: What is the article mainly about?
choices: How students grow vegetables in a garden
A contest that ended with a pizza party
A student program that reduced cafeteria trash
explanation: The article explains how the Green Team's composting program began, faced problems, and cut the trash in half.

passage:
The city of Venice, Italy, is famous for its canals, where boats replace cars and people travel along waterways instead of streets. Less well known, however, is what lies beneath the city's elegant buildings: millions of wooden posts driven deep into the mud.

Venice was founded on a group of small, marshy islands in a shallow lagoon. The soil there was far too soft to support heavy stone structures. To solve this problem, builders hammered long wooden posts, called piles, through the soft mud until they reached a firmer layer of packed clay and sand below. The piles were placed so close together that they formed a solid base. Workers then laid wooden platforms and stone slabs across the tops of the piles, and the buildings were constructed on these foundations.

At first glance, using wood seems like a poor choice. Wood left outdoors usually rots within a few decades, yet many of the piles beneath Venice have lasted for centuries. The explanation lies in the conditions underground. The piles are completely surrounded by mud and salt water, which contain very little oxygen. The fungi and bacteria that normally cause wood to decay need oxygen to survive, so they cannot easily attack the buried piles. Some researchers also believe that minerals from the water slowly soaked into the wood, making it harder.

Today, Venice faces serious challenges. The city has slowly sunk over the centuries while sea levels have risen, and floods have become more frequent. Engineers have built movable barriers at the entrances to the lagoon that can be raised when high tides threaten the city. Nevertheless, the ancient wooden foundations remain one of history's most ingenious solutions to the problem of building on unstable ground.

choices: To describe the history of boats in Venice
To compare Venice with other famous cities
To introduce the hidden foundations beneath Venice
To explain why cars are not allowed in Venice
explanation: Paragraph 1 points to "what lies beneath the city's elegant buildings," the topic of the rest of the passage.

passage:
If you look at the top of a tree stump, you will see a pattern of circles, one inside another. These circles, called growth rings, form because trees grow at different speeds during different seasons. In spring and early summer, when water is plentiful, a tree grows quickly and produces large cells with thin walls, which create a light-colored band. Later in the season, growth slows, and the tree produces smaller, thicker-walled cells that form a darker band. Together, one light band and one dark band represent a single year of growth.

Because of this pattern, counting the rings is a simple way to estimate a tree's age. However, the rings reveal much more than age. In a year with plenty of rain and mild temperatures, a tree usually forms a wide ring. In a year of drought, the ring is often very narrow. By measuring the width of each ring, scientists can learn about the climate of the past, long before people began keeping weather records.

The study of tree rings is called dendrochronology. Its founder, an American astronomer named A. E. Douglass, began studying rings in the early 1900s because he wanted to know whether changes in the sun affected Earth's weather. Although his original question was never fully answered, his method proved extremely useful in other fields.

For example, archaeologists use tree rings to date wooden objects. Since the trees in one region experience the same wet and dry years, they share a similar pattern of wide and narrow rings. By matching the pattern in an old wooden beam to a known record from the same region, researchers can determine the exact year in which the tree was cut down. This technique has helped to date ancient homes in the American Southwest with remarkable precision.
stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Archaeologists have found many ancient homes in the Southwest.
Trees grow faster in spring than in late summer.
A. E. Douglass proved that changes in the sun control the weather on Earth.
Tree rings show a tree's age and also give information about the past.
explanation: The passage explains how rings form, how they show age and past climate, and how they are used to date wooden objects.

If you look at the top of a tree stump, you will see a pattern of circles, one inside another. These circles, called growth rings, form because trees grow at different speeds during different seasons. In spring and early summer, when water is plentiful, a tree grows quickly and produces large cells with thin walls, which create a light-colored band. Later in the season, growth slows, and the tree produces smaller, thicker-walled cells that form a darker band. Together, one light band and one dark band represent a single year of growth.

Because of this pattern, counting the rings is a simple way to estimate a tree's age. However, the rings reveal much more than age. In a year with plenty of rain and mild temperatures, a tree usually forms a wide ring. In a year of drought, the ring is often very narrow. By measuring the width of each ring, scientists can learn about the climate of the past, long before people began keeping weather records.
